newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - Rubin tells Japan not to let surplus surge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rubin tells Japan not to let surplus surge.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin urged Japan on Friday to guard against a resurgence of its trade surplus, but rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency was the best way to do that.
Rubin told the American Chamber of Commerce here that Japan needed to promote strong domestic demand for its products, open up its markets further to imports and deregulate its economy.

"It is critical that Japan's current account surplus not rise again to a level that is detrimental to global growth, that causes trade friction with Japan's trading partners and that could fuel protectionist sentiments," he told the business leaders after meeting Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Japan's trade surplus rose in February for the first time in two years, as the weak yen helped make the nation's exports more competitive in world markets.
Speaking to reporters on his way here, Rubin made clear that he did not see a stronger yen -- and by inference a weaker dollar -- as the best way to contain and cut Japan's surplus.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," he said.

U.S. business leaders, though, made clear to Rubin that they were concerned about the weakness of the yen -- which has fallen some 50 percent against the dollar over the past two years, boosting Japanese competitiveness in the process.
"At current exchange rates, our profitability here is being killed," Robert Orr, director of government relations for Nippon Motorola Ltd, the local unit of Motorola Inc, told Rubin.
Rubin has consistently maintained that a strong dollar is in America's interests -- a stance he alluded to on Friday -- because it keeps down U.S inflation and interest rates.
But he has also recently taken to saying that the U.S. currency has been strong for some time, in an apparent effort to signal that he is not eager to see a further dollar advance.
The dollar did rise on Friday, though, poking over 123 yen as traders read Rubin's remarks as a sign that he would not actively push for a stronger yen.
Rubin told the business leaders that Japan's trade surplus "will take care of itself" if Tokyo promotes strong domestic demand and opens up and deregulates its economy.

The treasury chief called Hashimoto's recent wide-ranging deregulation package "impressive" but reserved judgment as to whether it would stimulate the economy enough to offset the economic drag from Japan's plans to sharply tighten its budget.
Some U.S. officials are worried that a rise in Japan's sales tax that took effect this week will sap demand at home and force Japanese companies to look abroad for sales.
Japanese officials said Hashimoto agreed with Rubin at their half-hour meeting that domestic demand-led growth was important for Japan, as it was for the United States.
The officials said Hashimoto reassured Rubin that Japan's surplus was unlikely to grow drastically and that the economic impact from the consumption tax rise would be limited.
Looking back over the past four years, Rubin said that both the United States and Japan had worked hard to iron out trade friction and strengthen their economic relationship.
He noted that Japan's current account surplus -- the broadest measure of trade -- has fallen from the equivalent of 3.1 percent of gross domestic product in 1993 to 1.4 percent.
A few years ago, Washington unsuccessfully tried to convince Tokyo to adopt a surplus target of one-and-a-half to two percent of gross domestic product.
But Rubin said on Friday that the United States did not have a target for the surplus now.
His visit to Japan comes on the heels of a series of recent trips to Tokyo by U.S. officials, including Vice President Al Gore and Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.
Rubin denied, though, that this represented a concerted U.S. strategy to turn up the heat on Japan.
He leaves Tokyo later on Friday for a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers in the Philippines.
